title: Five colors
hookLine: the five colors blind the eye; the sage cares for the belly, not the eye (Tao Te Ching 12)

cards: A phone screen at the end of a long day. Red badges. A video that starts on its own.

A banner sliding down over the banner you were reading. None of it is evil, and some of it is even interesting. And yet, after an hour of it, plain toast can taste like nothing, and a quiet room can feel strangely loud.
An old Chinese book, written long before any screen, has a short chapter about exactly this kind of tired: chapter twelve of the Tao Te Ching.

teach.b: First, the list. The five colors blind the eye, the chapter says. The five notes deafen the ear.
The five flavors dull the mouth. Racing and hunting drive the mind wild. Goods that are hard to get lead people astray.
Color, music, food, excitement, treasure: good things, every one. The problem is what too much of them does to the senses that take them in. Second, the strange result.

teach.h: MORE TO SEE, AND YOU SEE LESS.
teach.b: More color, and you see less. More sound, and you hear less. In the chapter's picture, the senses don't get sharper with more input; they go numb, like plain toast after sugar, or a quiet room after a loud one.
So the sage cares for the belly and not the eye.

teach.h: THE VOLUME KNOB, NOT THE RADIO.
teach.b: The belly here isn't about overeating; some translators read it as what a person actually needs, set against what only dazzles. The eye wants more to look at. The belly wants enough.

teach.h: LET GO OF THAT. TAKE HOLD OF THIS.
teach.b: Then a short instruction: let go of that, take hold of this. The chapter doesn't spell out which is which; some readers fill it in: that is the dazzle, this is the plain need underneath. Fourth, what it isn't saying.
It isn't telling anyone to hate color or give up music. Read this way, it's about the volume knob, not the radio: turn it down, and the senses can come back.

how: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter twelve as a reason to simplify their surroundings for a while: fewer screens, less noise, plainer food, to let the senses recover.

o: too much color and sound, until the senses go numb
the colors of the robes worn by Taoist monks
a painter's palette, in an old Chinese art

p: cares for the belly, not the eye

the chapter says more input leaves the senses numb
more color, and the eye sees less; more sound, and the ear hears less.

games.q: you're the sage in chapter twelve. there's a feast for the eyes on one side and plain food on the other. which do you care for?
o: the eye: more to look at.
both equally, as much as possible.
games.why: the sage cares for the belly and not the eye. let go of that, take hold of this.

practice: Turn down one thing right now: put the phone face down or in another room, turn off the music or the second screen, or dim a bright light.
Then sit with less coming in, and notice what the senses find once they're not flooded: a sound you hadn't heard, a color that was there all along, the taste in your mouth.

wordCard.voice: Five colors. Chapter twelve's picture of too much: color, sound and flavor that, piled up, leave the senses numb. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese: the five colors, the opening words of chapter twelve.

carryVoice: Your line: less to see. The eye wants more; the belly wants enough. That's chapter twelve.
